newsitem.title: JAPAN: Mazda mulls shared parts with Ford as ties deepen.
newsitem.headline: Mazda mulls shared parts with Ford as ties deepen.

text.p: Mazda Motor Corp said on Thursday it was exploring ways of sharing auto parts with Ford, signalling ever deeper ties with the U.S. auto giant under the leadership of Ford's Henry Wallace.
Mazda Motor Corp, which is one-third owned by Ford, is working on details of the cost-cutting collaboration and said it would decide on specifics by the end of March.

Mazda's long-standing ties with Ford intensified last year when Wallace, a Ford official seconded to Mazda, took over as president at the Japanese carmaker, setting himself the task of steering the troubled firm back to prosperity.
"We have plans to synchronise our cycle for launching new cars with that of Ford and to use common platforms," a Mazda spokesman said.

He said the company was looking at which models of cars should share standard platforms, and whether or not engines should be included in the shared-parts scheme. A platform comprises a chassis and suspension.
The standardisation will help Mazda's drive to improve business efficiency, the spokesman said.
In another sign of closer ties with Ford, the companies also plan to share a new computer network.

Mazda, Japan's fifth biggest carmaker, said it plans to spend 18 billion yen ($151 million) to build a computer network for three-dimensional product design and engineering as well as for production information. The network, to be completed by 2000, will connect Mazda, Ford and suppliers.
The question of standardising parts to cut costs was on the table before Ford raised its stake in Mazda last year, the spokesman said.

Ford increased its stake in Mazda to one-third from 24.54 percent last April, giving it management control. A few months later Wallace, a Ford official already seconded to Mazda, took the wheel, becoming the first foreigner to head a major Japanese firm.
The Hiroshima-based carmaker had been suffering slow exports due to the strong yen and sluggish domestic sales as a result of the weak economy and a lack of exciting new models.
Wallace has been reviewing Mazda's business, the spokesman said, including production of the mini passenger car the Carol, the company spokesman said, without elaborating.

A Japanese economic daily, the Nihon Keizai Shimbun, said earlier this year that Mazda would stop producing 660cc minivehicles next year as a way to reduce costs, procuring them instead under the Mazda brand from Suzuki Motor Corp.

Mazda posted a parent current profit of 2.08 billion yen ($17.4 million) in the six months to September 30, 1996, its first interim current profit after a string of losses. Current profit includes losses or gains on investments.

It expects its parent current profit to rise to 11 billion yen ($92.4 million) in the current business year, which ends in March, from 1.23 billion yen ($10.3 million) in 1995/96 -- thanks to sales of securities and cost-cutting.

In December, Mazda predicted its Japanese vehicle sales would rise 7.8 percent to 365,000 vehicles in calendar 1997 from the previous year and that its vehicle exports from Japan would rise 1.4 percent to 460,000 units, after a projected 3.0 percent rise in 1996. ($1=119 yen)
